analysis.one_liner: Requires public disclosure and court review of antitrust settlements and dropped cases.
analysis.headline: Nine Democratic senators back the bill, but it has seen no action since being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tightens the rules for how the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission settle or drop antitrust cases. It requires any proposed settlement or dismissal to be published and reviewed by a federal court, strengthens the standard courts use to judge whether a settlement truly serves the public, forces disclosure of contacts between enforcers and White House officials or defendants offering benefits, and lets state attorneys general take over federal antitrust cases the government tries to abandon. Its aim is to prevent large companies from quietly negotiating weak settlements or getting enforcement dropped.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, workers, and small businesses who pay the price of monopolization and anticompetitive mergers gain indirectly, because settlements could no longer be quietly watered down and dropped cases could be revived by state attorneys general [S2]. State attorneys general also gain a clear right to seek hearings, intervene, and substitute in as plaintiffs [S2]. Large companies lose the ability to settle on lenient terms or have cases dismissed without public scrutiny [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Any proposal by the Justice Department or FTC to voluntarily dismiss an antitrust case would have to be filed with the court and published in the Federal Register at least 45 days in advance, with the case stayed during that window, so the public can see when enforcement is being abandoned
During that window, any state attorney general could move to substitute in as plaintiff and continue the case, with the government required to hand over relevant litigation materials

Courts would have to find, based on evidence, that a proposed consent judgment is in the public interest, does not permit conduct that creates a material risk of violating the antitrust laws, and that its remedies are reasonably tailored to the alleged violations

The bill requires disclosure of communications between enforcement agencies and government officials including the Executive Office of the President, and lets courts order production of any benefits or concessions a defendant offered to the government, such as payments, donations, or policy changes connected to the case

In merger cases, parties would have to keep the merging assets separate for at least 15 days after the agency responds to public comments, with a court able to extend that if the settlement looks inadequate; the current public-comment process would also be shortened from 60 to 45 days but commenters would get a reply right

State attorneys general could request evidentiary hearings on settlements and, if granted, intervene, and courts would not have to defer to the government's own predictions about whether its remedies will work

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations under antitrust investigation, and companies seeking mergers, bear the cost: longer periods of holding assets separate, tougher settlement terms, more disclosure of their dealings with the government, and no more quiet dismissals of cases against them [S2]. The Justice Department and FTC also face new publication and response obligations [S2].

drawbacks.text: Companies with genuinely pro-competitive mergers would face at least 15 extra days of holding assets separate after public comments are answered, and courts could extend that period, adding deal costs and delay
The bill shortens the public comment period on settlements from 60 days to 45 days, giving the public somewhat less time even as it adds a reply stage

By directing courts not to defer to the government's predictions about whether its remedies will work, the bill invites judges with no enforcement expertise to second-guess settlement terms agencies negotiated

Requiring disclosure of every communication with officials including the Executive Office of the President, with dates and participants, could chill ordinary policy discussions between the White House and enforcement agencies

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The substantive benefits — settlements that courts actually test against the public interest, dismissals that cannot happen silently, and a paper trail on who got what from enforcement decisions — outweigh the added deal delay and disclosure burden, which fall on well-resourced corporations. The bill is procedurally focused rather than sweeping, so its real-world effect depends on courts using their new powers. The larger problem is that none of this takes effect: the bill has not moved at all since referral.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled, and it will die there if nothing happens before this Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the Antitrust Accountability and Transparency Act on March 17, 2026, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors: Durbin, Booker, Hirono, Blumenthal, Welch, Warren, Murphy, and Whitehouse
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary
That referral is the last action on the bill; the committee has taken up no hearing, markup, or vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies under antitrust investigation and their defense counsel are better off under the status quo: enforcement can still be settled on lenient terms or quietly dropped, and no court or state attorney general has any new power to challenge that.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

for.name: 8 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Durbin, Booker, Hirono, Blumenthal, Welch, Warren, Murphy, Whitehouse)

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Controls the committee agenda and has scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since its referral

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever been taken; all nine Senate backers are Democrats (9 of 45), and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee has left the bill untouched since referral.

industries.industry: Large corporations under antitrust investigation (dominant platforms, merging firms in tech, pharma, telecom, and retail)
industries.note: These companies currently benefit from the ability to negotiate lenient settlements or persuade the government to drop cases with little public scrutiny. The bill would force every settlement and dismissal into open court with a public-comment window, tougher judicial standards, disclosure of any benefits offered to officials, and a right for state attorneys general to take over dropped cases.

industries.industry: Corporate dealmakers and antitrust defense bar
industries.note: Mergers would face longer asset-hold-separate periods and a greater chance of judicial pushback on negotiated remedies, raising transaction costs. Some of that friction is the point of the bill, since weak remedies are how questionable deals get cleared.

The bill gives state enforcers a codified right to intervene in settlement reviews, request evidentiary hearings, and substitute in as plaintiffs when the federal government abandons a case, along with transfer of the underlying litigation materials.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is unlikely to advance: with no action beyond referral and only Democratic support in a Republican-run Senate, the realistic path is that it sits in the Judiciary Committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.
